q1.attribution: —Historian's account of the Great Depression as a global crisis, 1929–1939
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way the Depression spread beyond the United States according to the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the global severity of the Depression.
parts.c: Explain ONE political consequence of the Depression in an industrial democracy.

sample_answers.a: When American loans to Europe dried up after 1929, German and Austrian banks collapsed, transmitting the American financial crisis into a European banking crisis.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the gold standard, which forced countries to match each other's deflationary policies — no nation could reflate alone without losing gold, so contraction spread mechanically.
sample_answers.c: In the United States, the Depression discredited the old laissez-faire order and brought Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal — relief, public works, and financial regulation — expanding the federal government's economic role permanently.

q1.stimulus: The Depression began with an American stock market crash but became global through the mechanisms of an integrated economy: American loans to Europe dried up, collapsing German and Austrian banks; the U.S. Hawley-Smoot tariff of 1930 strangled world trade; and the gold standard transmitted deflation from country to country. By 1932, world industrial output had fallen by a third. The crisis discredited laissez-faire everywhere — and opened the door to Keynes, to the New Deal, and to dictators who promised work.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from President Franklin D. Roosevelt, First Inaugural Address, 1933
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Roosevelt makes in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the passage reflects the political challenge Roosevelt faced in 1933.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between Roosevelt's response to the Depression and the response of Britain's government in the early 1930s.

sample_answers.a: Roosevelt claims that fear itself — panic and loss of confidence — is the nation's greatest obstacle, and that action can turn retreat into advance.
sample_answers.b: In March 1933, with banks closed and a quarter of workers unemployed, his first task was psychological: restoring the public confidence on which banks, spending, and recovery depended.
sample_answers.c: Roosevelt launched large-scale federal relief, public works, and banking reform through the New Deal, while Britain's National Government pursued austerity — balanced budgets and retrenchment — with far less direct state intervention.

q2.stimulus: The only thing we have to fear is fear itself — nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance.

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE detail of the photograph.
parts.b: Explain ONE way photographs like Lange's were used by the U.S. government.
parts.c: Explain ONE cause of the rural migration shown in the photograph.

sample_answers.a: The photograph shows an anxious mother with a weathered face and hand to chin, children clinging to her shoulders and turned away — poverty made visible in a single family.
sample_answers.b: The Farm Security Administration hired photographers to document rural poverty, using images like this to build public support for New Deal relief programs for farmers and migrants.
sample_answers.c: One cause was the Dust Bowl: years of drought plus destructive farming practices destroyed Great Plains agriculture, driving hundreds of thousands west to California in search of farm work.

q3.stimulus: Dorothea Lange, 'Migrant Mother' (1936): a destitute pea-picker in California, Florence Owens Thompson, with her children — a Farm Security Administration photograph documenting Depression-era rural poverty.
